claims.claim: Tolkien's Foreword to Farmer Giles poses as the editor and translator of an ancient legend of the Little Kingdom, so the tale opens in the voice of a scholarly apparatus rather than a storyteller.
claims.source: Hammond & Scull, 'Farmer Giles of Ham' (Tolkien Estate)
claims.quote: pretends to be the editor and translator of an ancient legend

claims.claim: The Foreword declares the tale a translation from 'very insular Latin' of a compilation of old legends, establishing false provenance before any narrative begins.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Farmer Giles of Ham'
claims.quote: very insular Latin

claims.claim: The full Latin subtitle stacks offices and titles chancery-style (Lord of Tame, Count of Worminghall, King of the Little Kingdom), presaging the Latin-based jokes throughout.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Farmer Giles of Ham'
claims.quote: Count of Worminghall and King of the Little Kingdom

claims.claim: The Foreword solemnly discusses the document's nature (a late compilation from popular lays), its author (a local inhabitant writing long after the events, shown by his geographical knowledge) and the kingdom's boundaries in time and place, in the manner of a medieval-text editor's preface.
claims.source: Paul H. Kocher, Master of Middle-earth (1972), ch. VII
claims.quote: Solemnly he discusses the nature of the document

claims.claim: The Foreword fixes the Little Kingdom's date by placement within Geoffrey of Monmouth's chronology of Britain's partitions after Brutus and before Arthur, rather than by a number.
claims.source: Paul H. Kocher, Master of Middle-earth (1972), ch. VII
claims.quote: for a chronology of the many divisions within the island

claims.claim: Tolkien-as-translator voices the stock scholarly hope that the document will throw light on a dark period of history and on the origin of difficult place-names.
claims.source: Paul H. Kocher, Master of Middle-earth (1972), ch. VII
claims.quote: the usual pious hope of the scholar

claims.claim: The fictional compiler opens by looking back to a simpler past when there was more time, folk were fewer and villages were proud and independent, so the record voice is itself retrospective.
claims.source: Paul H. Kocher, Master of Middle-earth (1972), ch. VII
claims.quote: villages were proud and independent still in those days

claims.claim: When the record needs to say what a blunderbuss is, the compiler refers the question to the Four Wise Clerks of Oxenford, whose reply reproduces the Oxford English Dictionary definition word for word, embedding a modern reference-work register inside the chronicle.
claims.source: Paul H. Kocher, Master of Middle-earth (1972), ch. VII
claims.quote: corresponds word for word with the definition

claims.feature: irony turned on the cited authority
claims.claim: The narrator catches the OED's parenthesis about the blunderbuss being superseded 'in civilized countries' and remarks that Ham was not yet civilized enough for other weapons, turning the joke against the authorities cited.
claims.source: Paul H. Kocher, Master of Middle-earth (1972), ch. VII
claims.quote: rather turns the joke against the Dictionary editors

claims.claim: The tale closes with mock-learned derivations of Thame and Worminghall attributed to 'the learned in such matters', so place-name philology is the record's final word.
claims.source: Tom Shippey, The Road to Middle-earth, ch. 4 'A Cartographic Plot'
claims.quote: Thame with an h is a folly without warrant

claims.claim: Farmer Giles carries a two-layer apparatus in one short foreword: an imagined editor faults an imagined author's geography, though that author 'lived himself in the lands of the Little Kingdom'.
claims.source: Tom Shippey, The Road to Middle-earth, ch. 4 'A Cartographic Plot'
claims.quote: the imagined 'editor' of Farmer Giles to criticise its imagined 'author'

claims.claim: Distances and directions in the tale map onto real Oxfordshire places (Ham/Thame, Tamworth, Farthingho, the Rollright Stones) at a parochial scale, so the Little Kingdom is measured like a real county.
claims.source: Tom Shippey, The Road to Middle-earth, ch. 4 'A Cartographic Plot'
claims.quote: proof of the 'Little Kingdom's' lack of territorial ambition

claims.claim: The story's triumph of native over foreign is marked linguistically: in Giles's court the vulgar tongue came into fashion and none of his speeches were in Book-latin.
claims.source: Tom Shippey, The Road to Middle-earth, ch. 4 'A Cartographic Plot'
claims.quote: the vulgar tongue came into fashion

claims.claim: Throughout Farmer Giles linguistic humour is paramount, from Sunny Sam's gloomy proverbs and his misprision of the names Hilarius and Felix to Giles's own native errors of grammar.
claims.source: Tom Shippey, The Road to Middle-earth, ch. 4 'A Cartographic Plot'
claims.quote: linguistic humour is paramount

claims.claim: The Shire's Farthings descend from Farthingho in the Little Kingdom, and Thame and Worminghall are a long step beyond The Hobbit's bare 'The Hill' and 'The Water' toward the 600-plus named persons and places of The Lord of the Rings.
claims.source: Tom Shippey, The Road to Middle-earth, ch. 4 'A Cartographic Plot'
claims.quote: Farthingho set Tolkien thinking about the Farthings

claims.claim: The Farmer Giles chronicle fixes its events by the church calendar (St Nicholas' Day, Christmas Eve, 14 January) inside a legendary span 'between Brutus and King Arthur'.
claims.source: Noah Huisman, 'On Farmer Giles' (The Lumenorean)

claims.claim: Farmer Giles's pose as a translated manuscript with commentary on its origins and dubious place-name etymology parodies scholarly works including the Prologue to Tolkien's own Lord of the Rings, mocking the medieval appeal to authority.
claims.source: eNotes, 'Farmer Giles of Ham Analysis'
claims.quote: parody of scholarly works, including the prologue

claims.claim: The tale's narrator was 'Daddy' in the oral original, became 'the family jester', and took on a formal scholarly tone when the story was enlarged by half for an academic essay club in 1938.
claims.source: Hammond & Scull, 'Farmer Giles of Ham' (Tolkien Estate)
claims.quote: the family jester

claims.claim: By its 1949 publication the children's tale had acquired the mock-scholarly foreword, so the record register was a deliberate late addition rather than the story's native voice.
claims.source: Philip Irving Mitchell, 'Farmer Giles of Ham: Comedy in Faërie?' (DBU)
claims.quote: had acquired the mock-scholarly forward

claims.claim: Shippey identifies the Middle Kingdom of Farmer Giles with early Mercia, its capital possibly Tamworth, so the record's geography is a calque on real English history.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Farmer Giles of Ham'
claims.quote: based on early Mercia

claims.claim: Kullmann finds the Prologue imitates the non-fictional prose of nineteenth- and early-twentieth-century ethnography, while the Note on the Shire Records mimics works of historiography.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Editorial framing of The Lord of the Rings' (citing Kullmann & Siepmann 2021, pp. 46–47)
claims.quote: non-fictional prose of nineteenth- and early twentieth-century ethnography

claims.claim: 'Concerning Hobbits' places the text in the stylistic mode of nineteenth-century English antiquarianism, like a treatise on regional folklore, signalling to the reader a departure from modern novelistic conventions.
claims.source: John Halbrooks, 'Tolkienian Style' (Substack, 13 Mar 2024)
claims.quote: a certain strain of nineteenth-century English antiquarianism

claims.claim: Halbrooks argues Tolkien's greatest strength is that he very carefully adjusts his prose style and even his generic conventions according to the narrative circumstances.
claims.source: John Halbrooks, 'Tolkienian Style' (Substack, 13 Mar 2024)
claims.quote: he very carefully adjusts his prose style

claims.claim: The Shire is 'calqued' on England element by element: three founding tribes, a forgotten origin, founding brothers with horse-names, and a 272-year peace between battles matching the 270 years since Sedgemoor.
claims.source: Tom Shippey, The Road to Middle-earth, ch. 4 'A Cartographic Plot'
claims.quote: the Shire is 'calqued' on England

claims.claim: Organisationally the Shire, with its mayors, musters, moots and Shirriffs, is an old-fashioned and idealised England.
claims.source: Tom Shippey, The Road to Middle-earth, ch. 4 'A Cartographic Plot'
claims.quote: mayors, musters, moots and Shirriffs

claims.claim: Modern names are perceived as labels isomorphic with reality, so a dense name-stock weighs fantasy down with repeated implicit assurances that the things labelled exist; this is strongest in the Shire's map, account and history.
claims.source: Tom Shippey, The Road to Middle-earth, ch. 4 'A Cartographic Plot'
claims.quote: repeated implicit assurances of the existence of the things

claims.claim: Speakers in The Lord of the Rings have a strong tendency to talk like historical maps, reeling off names and river courses, a habit shared by Aragorn, Celeborn, Gimli, Gandalf and Meriadoc.
claims.source: Tom Shippey, The Road to Middle-earth, ch. 4 'A Cartographic Plot'
claims.quote: talk like maps, historical ones at that

claims.claim: The Prologue says 'pipe-weed' rather than tobacco because the imported word would sound wrong, and hedges its botany with a Latin binomial instead.
claims.source: Tom Shippey, The Road to Middle-earth
claims.quote: a variety probably of Nicotiana

claims.claim: The Note on the Shire Records credits Meriadoc with a Herblore of the Shire, a Reckoning of Years comparing calendars, and a treatise on Old Words and Names, so the record cites fictional reference works by title.
claims.source: Giuseppe Pezzini, 'The authors of Middle Earth' (J. Inklings Studies 2018), quoting the Note
claims.quote: Old Words and Names in the Shire

claims.claim: 'Concerning Pipe-weed' began as a lengthy speech by Merry in a draft of 'The Road to Isengard' that was removed and reworked into the Prologue, so dialogue was converted into record.
claims.source: Tolkien Gateway, 'Prologue (The Lord of the Rings)'
claims.quote: a lengthy speech of Merry about pipe-weed

claims.claim: A planned Prologue section on hobbit gift-giving customs and the ribadyan (birthday celebrant) was dropped as too lengthy.
claims.source: Tolkien Gateway, 'Prologue (The Lord of the Rings)'
claims.quote: being too lengthy

claims.feature: offices defined by what they actually do
claims.claim: The Prologue describes each office by its real function rather than its title: the Thain's office is largely ceremonial, the Mayor of Michel Delving is in practice Mayor of the Shire, and the Shirriffs' chief duty is rounding up stray livestock.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'The Shire'
claims.quote: rounding up stray livestock

claims.claim: The record marks the War of the Ring by a quantitative index, the rising number of Bounders, described as one of the few signs the hobbits had of the troubled time.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'The Shire'
claims.quote: one of the few signs for the hobbits

claims.claim: The Shire calendar is specified arithmetically: twelve months of thirty days plus five extra days, seven-day weeks, with Shire year 1 fixed to the founding in Third Age 1601.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'The Shire'

claims.claim: The Prologue defines the Thain by three institutions (Shire-moot, Shire-muster, Hobbitry-in-arms) and then hollows the office by noting that moots and musters had almost ceased to exist.
claims.source: A Tolkienist's Perspective, 'The Shire's Military Structure?'
claims.quote: had almost ceased to exist

claims.claim: The Prologue is a richly textured anthropology of the hobbits, delivered in an editorial voice of scholarly distance, and notes that hobbits liked books that set out what they already knew fair and square with no contradictions.
claims.source: Thomas J. West III, 'Tolkien Tuesdays: Re-Reading The Lord of the Rings: Prologue'
claims.quote: a richly-textured anthropology about the hobbits

claims.claim: In the Note on the Shire Records, as in the Prologue generally, Tolkien speaks in his own authorial persona as compiler and translator, stating that the account 'is drawn mainly from the Red Book' and that The Hobbit was 'already published'.
claims.source: Giuseppe Pezzini, 'The authors of Middle Earth' (J. Inklings Studies 2018)
claims.quote: speaking in his own authorial (hobbit) persona

claims.claim: Rather than silently changing The Hobbit's Gollum episode, Tolkien folded the revision into the record: the Red Book's first version rests on Bilbo's false account and later copies on the corrected one.
claims.source: CliffsNotes, 'Maps, Prologue, and Note on Shire Records'
claims.quote: incorporated the revisions directly into the story

claims.claim: The Prologue's rich historical detail and the convention of editing and translating a prior record ground the fantastic elements in realism and help the reader suspend disbelief.
claims.source: CliffsNotes, 'Maps, Prologue, and Note on Shire Records'
claims.quote: the feeling of rich historical detail

claims.claim: The Prologue's imitation of ethnography, comparable to eighteenth-century antiquarians such as William Stukeley and Thomas Percy, uses non-fiction techniques to make Middle-earth feel objectively real as well as subjectively experienced.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Storytelling in The Lord of the Rings'

claims.claim: The Note traces the Red Book through dated copies (the Thain's Book, IV 64; Findegil's exact copy, IV 172) and records the Minas Tirith annotations and corrections 'especially of names, words and quotations', a stemma written as prose.
claims.source: Giuseppe Pezzini, 'The authors of Middle Earth' (J. Inklings Studies 2018), quoting the Note
claims.quote: Findegil, King's Writer, finished this work in IV 172

claims.claim: Every stage of the Red Book's fictional transmission carries two datings, an Age-date and a Shire-reckoning equivalent, so the records cross-reference two calendars.
claims.source: Alexander Schmitt, 'Stages and Logic of the fictitious tradition of Tolkien's Legendarium' (schematax.org, 2021)

claims.claim: The Note states that the Tale of Years' dates are often conjectural, especially for the Second Age, so the record marks the limits of its own precision.
claims.source: Giuseppe Pezzini, 'The authors of Middle Earth' (J. Inklings Studies 2018), quoting the Note
claims.quote: the dates given are often conjectural

claims.claim: The Note localises its sources to specific libraries: Brandy Hall for Eriador and Rohan, Great Smials for Gondorian copies and summaries and as the place where the Tale of Years was put together.
claims.source: Giuseppe Pezzini, 'The authors of Middle Earth' (J. Inklings Studies 2018), quoting the Note
claims.quote: the libraries at Bucklebury and Tuckborough

claims.claim: Flieger holds that Tolkien inserted his own name on the title-page not as author but as the final transmitter/redactor, last in a line of transmitters, translators, redactors, scribes and copyists.
claims.source: Will Sherwood, 'Tolkien and the Age of Forgery', JTR 11.1 (2020), citing Flieger 2012
claims.quote: transmitters, translators, redactors, scribes, and copyists

claims.feature: antiquarian verbs on the title page
claims.claim: The Red Book's title-page vocabulary of 'compiled', 'observations', 'accounts' and 'translated' gives it the antiquarian air of Percy's Reliques, Macpherson's translations and Chatterton's Antiquities.
claims.source: Will Sherwood, 'Tolkien and the Age of Forgery', JTR 11.1 (2020)
claims.quote: 'compiled', 'observations', 'accounts' and 'translated'

claims.claim: The Red Book's history of interwoven, identifiable source-traditions and voices produces the effect of age and lends the text antiquarian authenticity.
claims.source: Will Sherwood, 'Tolkien and the Age of Forgery', JTR 11.1 (2020), citing Painter 2016
claims.quote: produce the effect of age

claims.claim: The antiquarian forger's toolkit that Groom lists for Chatterton (calligraphy, manuscripts, maps, heraldry, prefaces, footnotes, appendices, glossaries) is the same kit Tolkien uses to immerse readers in Arda.
claims.source: Will Sherwood, 'Tolkien and the Age of Forgery', JTR 11.1 (2020), citing Groom 2014
claims.quote: prefaces, footnotes, appendices, and glossaries

claims.claim: Richard C. West calls the Red Book a spurious source whose authority appeals not to the old and familiar but to the modern mystique of scholarly research.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Red Book of Westmarch'
claims.quote: the modern mystique of scholarly research

claims.claim: Kristin Thompson identifies the Red Book as a found-manuscript conceit in the line running back to Samuel Richardson's eighteenth-century novels.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Red Book of Westmarch'
claims.quote: found manuscript conceit

claims.claim: Flieger describes The Lord of the Rings as presented at four levels at once: the story itself, a version referencing other versions, a historical artifact (the Red Book), and a modern edition complete with scholarly and critical apparatus.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Interrupted Music'
claims.quote: complete with scholarly and critical apparatus

claims.claim: Tolkien went to elaborate lengths to construct a credible book tradition, with repeated mentions of Bilbo's diary, his Translations from the Elvish, and masses of notes in his room at Rivendell.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Tolkien's frame stories' (citing Flieger)
claims.quote: credible book tradition

claims.claim: Flieger finds The Hobbit's frame rather fragile because its narrator often speaks in a voice that cannot be Bilbo's, whereas The Lord of the Rings has the frame carefully embedded from the earliest drafts.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Tolkien's frame stories' (citing Flieger)
claims.page: § The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings
claims.quote: rather fragile

claims.claim: Appendix A's Kings of the Mark section uses annalistic headings, dates recording great events, and later editor's footnotes (such as identifying Holdwine as Meriadoc), giving the look of authentic historical documentation.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Tolkien's frame stories'

claims.claim: Brljak argues that the pseudo-editorial, pseudo-philological and pseudo-translational framework is both the cornerstone and crowning achievement of Tolkien's mature literary work, modelled on the impression of depth he admired in Beowulf.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Editorial framing of The Lord of the Rings'
claims.quote: pseudo-editorial, pseudo-philological, and pseudo-translational

claims.claim: Turner notes the frame works at two levels at once, treating the world of the story as historical fact while creating for the reader the illusion of a direct link through time and space.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Editorial framing of The Lord of the Rings' (citing Turner)
claims.quote: the world of the story as historical fact

claims.claim: Pezzini argues the meta-textual frame lets Tolkien write in contrasting styles, alternating between high and low, and to dignify the humble while writing in the low style.
claims.source: Bradley Birzer, 'How Did Tolkien Write Great Books?' (Law & Liberty, reviewing Pezzini)
claims.quote: alternating between high and low, transcendent and earthy

claims.claim: Pezzini describes the Red Book as an authorial mosaic (Bilbo, Frodo, Sam as last hand) stitched into the narration by 'remembering formulas' such as 'Pippin afterwards recalled little' and by reportorial scenes where separated hobbits recount what they witnessed.
claims.source: Erik Jampa Andersson, 'The Red Book: Giuseppe Pezzini on Tolkien's Meta-Textual Frame' (Substack, lecture notes)
claims.quote: Pippin afterwards recalled little

claims.claim: The translator persona of Appendix F would rather change the English language and coin new words than deliver a substandard translation, so consistency of rendering governs the whole record.
claims.source: N. Lurquin, 'Translating the Red Book of Westmarch' (Tolkien: Medieval and Modern blog)
claims.quote: rather change the English language and make new words

claims.claim: Groom places Tolkien in the English antiquarian line of Swift, Chatterton and Stukeley as one who enlists the aesthetics of antiquarianism, and Sherwood reads the non-narrative elements as Tolkien improving on antiquarian forgery to create modern fantasy's conventions.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Tolkien and antiquarianism'
claims.page: § Tolkien in the English antiquarian tradition
claims.quote: enlists the aesthetics of antiquarianism

claims.claim: Tolkien describes heraldic devices for characters and nations in simple English rather than technical blazon, keeping the record's technical matter in ordinary diction.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Tolkien and antiquarianism'

claims.feature: Appendix F rationale for register layering
claims.claim: In Appendix F the translator explains that Westron is rendered as English to preserve the contrast between a widespread language and the living remains of far older and more reverend tongues, with the analogy that calling Rivendell Imladris would be like speaking of Winchester as Camelot.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Pseudotranslation in The Lord of the Rings'
claims.quote: far older and more reverend tongues

claims.claim: Turner observes that Tolkien's Winchester/Camelot analogy further blurs the already confused distinction between fiction and reality that the pseudotranslation sets up.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Pseudotranslation in The Lord of the Rings' (citing Turner)
claims.quote: further blurs the already confused distinction

claims.claim: Appendix A opens with a key to its own apparatus: actual extracts from longer annals and tales are placed within quotation marks, later insertions in brackets, notes within quotation marks come from the sources and others are editorial.
claims.source: Giuseppe Pezzini, 'The authors of Middle Earth' (J. Inklings Studies 2018), n. 35 quoting Appendix A
claims.quote: Insertions of later date are enclosed in brackets

claims.feature: narrative formulas imply hobbit or Gondorian authorship
claims.claim: Formulas such as 'before we came to the Shire' imply parts of the Appendices are written by hobbits, while 'as we have learned from the King' points to Gondor and the scribe Findegil, so the annal's first person shifts with its source.
claims.source: Giuseppe Pezzini, 'The authors of Middle Earth' (J. Inklings Studies 2018)
claims.quote: as we have learned from the King

claims.claim: Appendix A declares that only selections from its sources, in most places much abridged, are presented, so the annal frames itself as an epitome of fuller documents.
claims.source: Giuseppe Pezzini, 'The authors of Middle Earth' (J. Inklings Studies 2018), n. 34 quoting Appendix A
claims.quote: in most places much abridged

claims.claim: The appendices are full of scribal glosses, later notes and editorial references deliberately matched to the textual history in the Note on the Shire Records, so the frame is realised by formal features rather than asserted.
claims.source: Giuseppe Pezzini, 'The authors of Middle Earth' (J. Inklings Studies 2018)
claims.quote: full of scribal glosses, later notes, and editorial references

claims.claim: Turner describes the prologue and appendices as an elaborate apparatus containing genealogies and ancient annals complete with scribal footnotes and editorial comments, even a discussion 'On Translation'.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Literary devices in The Lord of the Rings' (citing Turner 2011)

claims.claim: Passages of Appendix A translated from Fourth-Age hobbit or Gondorian writers are marked only by surrounding quotation marks, expecting the reader to recall the Prologue's discussion of sources.
claims.source: Kate Nepveu, 'LotR re-read: Appendices' (Reactor)
claims.quote: only marked by surrounding quotation marks

claims.claim: Some quoted passages in Appendix A let Tolkien suggest things without committing to them, in the chronicle idiom 'some say he dwells there still'.
claims.source: Kate Nepveu, 'LotR re-read: Appendices' (Reactor)
claims.quote: some say he dwells there still

claims.claim: Appendix A's narrative annals and Appendix B's year-list divide one history so that a reader loses orientation in A and finds B redundant, wanting something more like A and B combined.
claims.source: Kate Nepveu, 'LotR re-read: Appendices' (Reactor)
claims.quote: something more like A & B combined

claims.claim: Appendix B primarily contains timelines (lists of years) for the Second, Third and Fourth Ages with only a few brief narrative sections, such as the account of the Wizards.
claims.source: Tolkien Gateway, 'Appendix B'
claims.quote: a few brief narrative sections

claims.claim: The Fourth-Age section of the Tale of Years gives its dates in Shire-reckoning and follows primarily what happened to the hobbits, so the calendar and focus track the compiler's own community.
claims.source: Tolkien Gateway, 'Appendix B'
claims.quote: dates are given in the Shire-reckoning

claims.claim: Annals are lists of years or spans with brief summaries, and Tolkien's Second Age annals have significant gaps, a single entry covering the years 2000 to 3000.
claims.source: Norbert Schürer, 'Second Age, Middle Age', JTR 15.2 (2022)
claims.quote: lists of years or spans with brief summaries

claims.claim: Appendix B's Second Age opens by declaring that of events in Middle-earth the records are few and brief and their dates often uncertain, so the annalist states the limits of his sources before listing them.
claims.source: Norbert Schürer, 'Second Age, Middle Age', JTR 15.2 (2022), quoting Appendix B
claims.quote: the records are few and brief

claims.feature: annals versus Tales as two modes
claims.claim: Tolkien told Waldman that the Rings of Power and the Downfall of Númenor were dealt with annalistically and in two Tales or Accounts, naming a two-mode scheme of compressed annal and expanded tale.
claims.source: Norbert Schürer, 'Second Age, Middle Age', JTR 15.2 (2022), quoting Letter 131
claims.quote: dealt with annalistically, and in two Tales or Accounts

claims.claim: Tolkien's annals are modelled on the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, with entries opening 'Here' or 'In this year', and his Old English versions use the early West Saxon dialect of the Chronicle's earliest parts.
claims.source: Himring, 'Fingon's rescue of Maedhros in Old English' (Silmarillion Writers' Guild)
claims.quote: early West Saxon (second half of the ninth century)

claims.claim: The Silmarillion uses a compressed style in which events are briefly documented as if in annals recording history and legend, with minimal dialogue, which makes it feel more distant and difficult.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Tolkien's prose style'
claims.quote: as if in annals recording history and legend

claims.feature: varying styles as a depth factor
claims.claim: Drout, Hitotsubashi and Scavera identify four factors behind the impression of depth, the fourth being different texts written in varying styles as if by different hands.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Literary devices in The Lord of the Rings'
claims.quote: Different texts written in varying styles

claims.claim: Sipahi highlights the Prologue's device of multiple manuscripts, redactions and translations of the Red Book as the framework that establishes authenticity, while Brooke-Rose dismissed the genealogies and histories as unnecessary to the narrative.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Impression of depth in The Lord of the Rings'

claims.claim: Bowman shows Tolkien blurring the line between story and history in the Appendices, following his stated preference for history, true or feigned.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'The Tale of Aragorn and Arwen'
claims.quote: history, true or feigned

claims.claim: The Tale of Aragorn and Arwen is attributed within the frame to Barahir, grandson of Faramir, writing after Aragorn's death, with an abbreviated version entered in the Thain's Book by Findegil.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'The Tale of Aragorn and Arwen'
claims.quote: written after Aragorn's death by Barahir

claims.claim: Barkley argues the main part of the Tale is narrated by Aragorn and Armstrong considers Arwen as narrator after his death, so the annal admits embedded first-person witnesses within an editorial frame.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'The Tale of Aragorn and Arwen'
claims.quote: narrated by Aragorn

claims.claim: Appendix A reads like a real history because its narrative style is that of a historian summarising primary documents rather than a novelist.
claims.source: Tolkien Geek, 'Appendix A (Part One)'
claims.quote: reads like a real history

claims.claim: The Appendices function as a guidebook to the relics of Middle-earth's history and, in Tolkien's own words quoted by Gray, played a very large part in readers' pleasure.
claims.source: Richard Gray, 'The Read Goes Ever On: Appendices' (The Reel Bits)
claims.quote: a guidebook to those relics

claims.claim: Siepmann's corpus comparison finds Tolkien uses roughly twice the nineteenth-century key words of his baseline and sets modern words inside nineteenth-century structural patterns so that common English words are rendered strange.
claims.source: Sharon L. Bolding, review of Kullmann & Siepmann, Mythlore 41.1 (2022)
claims.quote: common English words are rendered strange

claims.claim: Kullmann's character-by-character stylistics finds Gandalf and Frodo the most flexible registers, Sam the most evolving, Gimli and Legolas the most traditional, and Merry and Pippin speaking common English as reality-based touchstones.
claims.source: Sharon L. Bolding, review of Kullmann & Siepmann, Mythlore 41.1 (2022)
claims.quote: reality-based touchstones

claims.claim: Shippey reports Tolkien's working rule that one should always start with a name, because a name produces a story, which underlies the place-name etymologies that open and close his civic records.
claims.source: Tom Shippey, 'J.R.R. Tolkien and Philology' (Tolkien Estate)
claims.quote: Give me a name and it produces a story
